stem: A client newly prescribed rifampin asks about an expected visible medication effect that may occur during therapy. Which teaching is appropriate?

options.A: A complete loss of taste is expected with otherwise uncomplicated rifampin therapy
options.B: Urine, sweat, tears, saliva, and other secretions may become orange-red or brownish-red
options.C: Rifampin does not cause visible color changes in body fluids
options.D: Permanent darkening of tooth enamel routinely occurs in every client

rationale: Rifampin labeling warns patients that the drug may discolor body fluids and secretions yellow, orange, red, or brown; urine, sweat, tears, sputum/saliva and other secretions may be affected. Soft contact lenses may become permanently stained. B is correct.
educational_objective: Teach clients the expected rifampin-associated discoloration of body fluids and secretions.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine (official FDA drug labeling)
source_locator: Information for Patients — discoloration of teeth, urine, sweat, sputum, and tears; soft contact lens staining
source_claim_supported: Rifampin may produce yellow/orange/red/brown discoloration of body fluids and secretions; soft contact lenses can be permanently stained.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication effects and client education
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — rifampin client teaching

source_original.stem: A client newly prescribed rifampin for tuberculosis asks the nurse about a common, harmless side effect they may notice. The nurse should explain that rifampin commonly causes:

options.A: A complete loss of taste that commonly develops during otherwise uncomplicated rifampin therapy
options.B: Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, tears, or saliva that is expected with rifampin
options.C: No visible change in any body fluid because rifampin does not alter secretion coloration
options.D: Permanent dark discoloration of tooth enamel that routinely occurs during rifampin treatment

source_original.rationale: Rifampin commonly causes a harmless orange-red discoloration of body fluids, including urine, sweat, tears, and saliva. Clients should be informed of this expected effect in advance to prevent unnecessary alarm, and those who wear soft contact lenses should be cautioned that the lenses may become permanently stained.
source_original.source_detail: Rifampin patient information: orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, tears, saliva and possible contact-lens staining; reviewed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the generic FDA label directory with a product-specific DailyMed patient-information locator and avoided calling every discoloration 'harmless' without context. Retained the expected rifampin color-change teaching and contact-lens caution in the rationale.

audit_findings.source_authority: Official DailyMed rifampin label; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: Current DailyMed rifampin patient-information labeling checked 2026-08-17.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Body-fluid/secretions discoloration and soft-contact-lens staining are directly supported by the label.

distractor_audit.A: Complete taste loss is not the expected teaching point.
distractor_audit.D: Overstates tooth discoloration as permanent and routine for every client.

audit_findings.cueing: Removed 'common, harmless side effect' phrasing and asked for expected visible medication effect.
audit_findings.blueprint: Medication teaching fits Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked DailyMed patient information; B remains uniquely correct.
